clue.text: Border protest?

blocks.note: first meaning: a frontier region, as in the Welsh or Scottish borderlands
second meaning: a demonstration where people walk together in public

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a dispute over a frontier, but they are two separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A march is historically a frontier district, and also a walking demonstration by campaigners.

clue.text: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont

definitions.text: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont

blocks.clueFragment: Sweet sleeper on a bank at Belmont
blocks.note: surface reading: a lovely person napping on a riverbank
setter's reading: Lorenzo's line in The Merchant of Venice, set at Portia's house in Belmont

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, Act 5, at Belmont: 'How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!'
explanation.definitionFit: In the play the night light from the sky is said to rest sweetly on the slope, so it is the sleeper.

clue.text: Old king demanding shelter, say ?

indicators.note: say asks for the words to be spoken, so the sound of the request matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: a plea to be given cover overhead

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch insists on being given a roof over his head.
explanation.walkthrough: William II of England was nicknamed William Rufus.
explanation.definitionFit: William Rufus, son of the Conqueror, ruled England from 1087 to 1100, an early monarch.

clue.text: For French company inside worker, a plantation

indicators.note: inside puts the firm's abbreviation within the word for a labourer

blocks.note: a farm hand or factory hand
short for Compagnie, the French equivalent of Co
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French firm places a labourer on an estate overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacienda is a large estate or plantation in Spanish-speaking countries, usually with a main house.

clue.text: Died at the end of a game of croquet

definitions.text: at the end of a game of croquet
definitions.note: describes what a ball has done, a past participle like the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: an informal phrase for passed away

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of a game of croquet
blocks.note: second meaning: in croquet a ball finishes by striking the central peg

explanation.surface: Someone expires just as the last croquet game finishes on the lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase means expired, and in croquet a ball that hits the final peg has completed its course and leaves play.

clue.text: Top dog, 'tis said

indicators.note: 'tis said means it is spoken, so the word is judged by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: a Peke is short for a Pekinese, a small dog

explanation.surface: Someone is rumoured to be the boss, the top dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' reads as one phrase meaning leader; split it, and 'Top' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The peak is the highest point or summit, so it is the top of a mountain or anything else.

clue.text: Agree talks perhaps for Gitche Gumee etc.

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words could take another form, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: both words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Negotiators might settle on a name for Longfellow's big-sea-water.
explanation.walkthrough: Gitche Gumee is the name in Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha for Lake Superior.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Superior and its four neighbours form the chain of huge freshwater bodies on the US-Canada border, so 'etc.' widens one to the set.

clue.text: Oriental flower festival

blocks.note: first meaning: whimsically, something that flows east, as a river might
second meaning: the Christian spring feast of the Resurrection

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a crossword favourite for something that flows, such as a river; one flowing east would be an east-er.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the main spring holy day of the Christian calendar, and the word also reads as east plus -er for a flowing thing.

clue.text: Is it the President's place to go thus in his enthusiasm?

definitions.text: Is it the President's place to go thus in his enthusiasm?

blocks.clueFragment: Is it the President's place to go thus in his enthusiasm?
blocks.note: surface reading: a question about whether a head of state should get carried away
setter's reading: a company president sits above the directors, so his place is literally above them

explanation.walkthrough: To go overboard is to be excessively enthusiastic; a president's position is over the board of directors.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for going too far through excitement, read literally, describes a chairman ranking above his directors.

clue.text: Heavyweight not up on points

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word climbs the column and is read from its last letter

blocks.note: taken as written
north and east, two compass points

explanation.surface: A big boxer refuses to win on a points decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A metric ton of a thousand kilograms is a large unit of mass, a weight that is heavy.

clue.text: This I have somehow to face if I do the honours

indicators.note: somehow says the following words are managed by some unstated method, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the four words taken letter for letter as raw material

explanation.surface: A reluctant host admits there is something to be faced whenever they act as master of ceremonies.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder sits in the middle of the clue; 'This I have' just introduces it.
explanation.definitionFit: To officiate is to perform a formal duty at a ceremony, which is what someone doing the honours undertakes.

clue.text: Jack's back thrice, in opposite directions

indicators.note: in places the word for thrice inside the pair of compass letters, between them

blocks.note: south and north are opposite points of the compass
Latin for three times, used in music and prescriptions

explanation.surface: A sailor's back has been put out three times, twisting in opposite directions.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is a sailor (a jack tar), so his back is the back of his ship. TER is Latin for thrice.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern is the rear part of a ship, so it is the back end of a seaman's vessel.

clue.text: Hark ye-money is returned free from deduction

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word after it is read from its end

blocks.note: L, from Latin libra, is the pound sterling
taken as written
a net sum is what remains with nothing deducted

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned call to attention announcing that money is being refunded without deductions.
explanation.definitionFit: Hark ye is an archaic command to pay attention, the same as the imperative telling someone to hear.

clue.text: Malt beer brew gets us shaking

indicators.note: to brew is to mix ingredients and let them work, so these letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: the two words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Drinking strong home-brewed malt beer leaves the drinkers unsteady and trembling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brew' looks like a noun after malt beer, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Atremble is a literary adjective for quivering, so it can stand in for shaking as a description of someone.

clue.text: Seize contentious point (a merry thought?)

blocks.note: to collar a suspect is to grab him
a bone of contention

explanation.surface: Someone grabs hold of a disputed issue, perhaps with a cheerful idea in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: A merrythought is the wishbone of a bird, formed from its fused clavicles; the question mark admits this is a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: In birds the wishbone, traditionally called the merrythought, is the fused pair of clavicles, so it is an example.

clue.text: All those thousands of American dollars?

definitions.text: All those thousands of American dollars?

blocks.clueFragment: All those thousands of American dollars?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone asks about a large pile of money from America
setter's reading: in American slang a thousand dollars has its own word, and adding them all up gives the full sum

explanation.walkthrough: A grand is slang for a thousand dollars, so the sum of all those thousands is playfully a total of grands.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the final sum reached after adding every figure, which is what 'all' of a set of amounts comes to.

clue.text: Presumption of damage to gear on car

indicators.note: damage knocks the words out of shape, so their letters end up in a new order

blocks.note: the three words used letter for letter

explanation.surface: A garage assumes a damaged gearbox is the motorist's fault.
explanation.definitionFit: Presumption is overbearing boldness, taking liberties, which is a close synonym for haughty pride.

clue.text: The load, one hears, must take its turn

indicators.note: one hears says the word is caught by the ear, so its sound counts rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a load is a weight carried

explanation.surface: Cargo is told it has to queue its turn before being shifted.
explanation.definitionFit: To wait is to hold back until one's place in a queue or sequence arrives.

clue.text: A heath plant hill men cultivate no end

indicators.note: no end means the final letter of the word for cultivate is dropped

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
taken as written
to till is to plough and work soil

explanation.surface: Hill farmers grow a moorland plant without stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Tormentil is a small yellow-flowered potentilla that grows on heaths and moors, so it is one such plant.

clue.text: Car spy loses her hair with unintelligent workers

indicators.note: loses means part of the name goes, and her hair sounds like the part dropped

blocks.note: short for automobile
Mata Hari, the First World War dancer and spy

explanation.surface: A female agent in a car is shorn of her locks alongside some dim workers.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part of Mata Hari's name sounds like 'hairy', so 'her hair' is what she loses.
explanation.definitionFit: Automata are self-operating machines or robots, which work mechanically without any thought of their own.

clue.text: A wrong to right

blocks.note: surface reading: an injustice that ought to be corrected
setter's reading: the legal term for a civil wrong that a court can put right with damages

explanation.walkthrough: In law this word means a civil wrong, such as negligence or trespass, for which the courts award a remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal term names a civil injury, which is precisely a wrong that the claimant asks a court to remedy.

clue.text: Unhappy crime? It's a scream!

blocks.note: feeling blue is feeling down
the gravest crime

explanation.surface: A sad killing is greeted with shrieks, or perhaps with laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a scream' suggests a joke; here the answer is a scream, as in the phrase to scream it.
explanation.definitionFit: To shout this phrase is to make a loud, shrill outcry, so the phrase itself is a kind of scream.

clue.text: Ambled confusedly about the scene of uproar

indicators.note: confusedly says the word is jumbled, so its letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: the word used letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone wanders dazedly around the site of a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedlam was the old name of Bethlem, London's hospital for the insane, hence a place of chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam names a place or state of wild noise and confusion, after the old London asylum.

clue.text: This O type photograph was his invention

definitions.text: This O type photograph was his invention

blocks.note: surface reading: some kind of photograph of type O
setter's reading: the inventor's name followed by O and TYPE spells the early photograph named after him

explanation.walkthrough: Louis Daguerre invented the daguerreotype, an early photograph on a silvered plate; add O and TYPE to his name and you have it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French pioneer of photography gave his surname to the process he invented in 1839.

clue.text: Cubed root of carrots?

blocks.note: surface reading: mathematics, a cube root
setter's reading: carrots are a root vegetable, and the cook chops them into small cubes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cubed root' points at arithmetic; the root is actually the vegetable, chopped up in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting vegetables into small cubes is exactly what this cooking term describes.

clue.text: Satirist's call to the nation

blocks.note: a shout to attract attention
a people or nation

explanation.surface: A satirical writer issues a public appeal to his country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet wrote the Satires, so he is a classic example of a satirist.

clue.text: Through this way to Tipperary.

blocks.note: first meaning: by way of, onward
second meaning: the song says it's a long way to Tipperary, split into two words

explanation.walkthrough: The First World War song: 'It's a long way to Tipperary', a county town in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Along means onward through or by the length of something, and split as two words it is the song's description of the way.

clue.text: Those of 1 Across saw Caesar off

definitions.text: Those of 1 Across saw Caesar off

blocks.note: surface reading: something belonging to a particular month
setter's reading: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the fifteenth of that month, as the soothsayer warned

explanation.walkthrough: 1 Across is a month here; 'Beware the ides of March' warns Caesar in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar these are the middle days of a month, the fifteenth of March being Caesar's death day.

clue.text: Is it possible for a new driver to get in a groove?

blocks.note: asking whether one can
the article kept
a learner driver shows an L plate

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a novice motorist can settle into a routine.
explanation.walkthrough: A learner driver in Britain displays an L plate, so a new driver is L.
explanation.definitionFit: A canal can be a channel or furrow, as in anatomy's ear canal, so it serves as a groove.

clue.text: He's not even sacked?

blocks.note: an odd number is not even
a male person
dismissed from a job

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a man has escaped the dismissals that hit everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the one who does not fit with the rest of a group, the single exception left over.

clue.text: Unlike the sleep of Joel's old men

definitions.text: Unlike the sleep of Joel's old men

blocks.clueFragment: Unlike the sleep of Joel's old men
blocks.note: surface reading: a comparison with how elderly men sleep
setter's reading: the prophet Joel says your old men shall see visions at night, so a sleep unlike theirs has none

explanation.walkthrough: Joel 2:28 in the Bible: 'your old men shall dream dreams'. A sleep unlike theirs has no visions.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes sleep without visions, the opposite of the night of the old men in the prophecy.

clue.text: A star in computer language

blocks.note: first meaning: the variable star Beta Persei, the Demon Star
second meaning: the algorithmic programming language devised in 1958

explanation.surface: A celebrity is somehow embedded in programming code.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a famous eclipsing star in Perseus and to an early algorithmic programming language.
